reference: Fringe benefits tax regime is essentially a tax on a wide range of benefits provided by an employer to an employee. This tax is payable by the employer, not the employee, because the benefit is received from the employment. There are a number of different types of fringe benefit, which all fall within these two categories.In this case, the fringe benefit is taxable because it falls within one of these two categories. A de minimis benefit is a minor, trivial benefit that can be given to an employee without it being classified as a fringe benefit. It is called a de minimis benefit because the value of the benefit is so small that it is unimportant. In practice, de minimis benefits are usually related to the workplace, such as a birthday cake or a cup of coffee. They are not subject to FBT because they are not significant enough to constitute a benefit.A benefit that is given to supervisory employees is also taxable. These benefits are treated differently under the FBTAA because they are given to employees who have some level of responsibility for managing other employees.Benefits provided to rank and file employees are also taxable. These benefits are generally given to employees who do not have any level of responsibility for managing other employees.Benefits given in the form of insurance or retirement benefits plan are also taxable.An employer may provide an employee with a range of benefits from which the employee chooses the benefit that best suits the employee’s needs. For example, an employee might be able to choose between an additional week of annual leave and a one-off payment of $5000.The option e is the correct answer because it supports employees education. This is a taxable fringe benefit. Employers are encouraged to provide educational assistance to their employees because it helps to increase the skill levels of the workforce and improve productivity. The residency test is used to determine the tax residency status of a company in Australia. There are four tests that a company can satisfy to be considered a tax resident of Australia under the residency test: the place of incorporation test, the central management and control test, the controlling shareholder test, or the nexus test.

The place of incorporation test is satisfied if the company is incorporated or formed in Australia or if it is an Australian resident for tax purposes. The central management and control test is satisfied if the company's central management and control is in Australia. The controlling shareholder test is satisfied if a majority of the company's voting power is held by shareholders who are residents of Australia or if a person who is a resident of Australia has a controlling interest in the company. The nexus test is satisfied if the company has a substantive connection with Australia.

Therefore, a company can be considered a tax resident of Australia under the residency test if it satisfies any one of the four tests. This means that the correct answer is Option D: any of the above.

The benefit must be provided by an employer, an associate of the employer, or a third party under an arrangement with the employer or associate of the employer. The benefit must also be in respect of the employment of the employee. This means that the benefit must be related to the employment of the employee or associate of the employer.

In FCT v Holmes 95 ATC 4476, it was held that where a taxpayer enters into an agreement to make periodic payments to another entity, the critical question is whether the payments are consideration for a transferable right to receive income or capital. Option E: IRC v Ramsay [1953] 1 All ER 847 illustrates the difficulty when distinguishing between annuities and installment payments for the fixed price of a capital asset. In this case, the issue was whether a series of payments made by a taxpayer to an insurance company in exchange for a life insurance policy was an annuity or a series of installment payments. The court held that the payments were an annuity, despite the fact that the amount of each payment was fixed, because the payments were made in consideration of the life insurance policy and not in consideration of the sale of the capital asset. Therefore, the fixed nature of the payments did not make them an annuity.

This case illustrates the difficulty of distinguishing between annuities and installment payments for the fixed price of a capital asset. In general, an annuity is a series of payments made periodically over a period of time, while an installment payment is a series of payments made over a period of time in exchange for the sale of a capital asset. However, in some cases, it may be difficult to determine whether a series of payments is an annuity or an installment payment, particularly when the payments are made in exchange for a life insurance policy or some other financial product. In such cases, the distinction between annuities and installment payments may turn on the specific facts and circumstances of the case.
